pr_title: debug: analyzer: fix incorrect cpu cycle counts
pr_body:
The existing CPU cycle counts do not handle unsigned integer rollover
when taking the diff from previous cycles.

The existing cycles do not reset for the next analyzer interval.
This causes excessive accumulation of execution cycles and does not
provide an accurate run-time usage statistic.

This patch addresses these bugs by implementing runtime_stats_clear
functions for use by the thread analyser, and calculates the difference
from last_switched_cycles with the rollover case.

Fixes #37521 

Signed-off-by: Arien Judge <arienjudge@outlook.com>

issue_context.title: debug: analyzer: produces nonsense CPU usage statistics
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
Thread Analyser reports impossible cycle usage numbers.
Three issues are causing this behaviour:
* Execution cycle stats aren't being reset appropriately on interval expiry - leading to erroneous accumulation of cycles
* Cycle count subtraction isn't handling integer rollover correctly

This can be solved by handling uint32_t subtraction edge cases correctly, and ensuring execution cycles are reset each interval

**To Reproduce**
* Using a nucleo_h753zi
* Configure thread analyser and thread runtime stats. 
  * Configuring ethernet and loading network with multicast introduces sufficient load on rx_q thread for observation

  ```
  CONFIG_THREAD_ANALYZER=y
  CONFIG_THREAD_RUNTIME_STATS=y
  ```

* Load project and observe thread output.

**Expected behavior**
Expect sensible CPU stats as a percentage of runtime over the last analyser interval. Percentages should sum to 100% (or close due to integer flooring

review_comments: can you explain why you have to clear the counters on every iteration of the thread analyzer? Wouldn't this only show stats since last print?

That's correct. I find measuring stats over a well defined interval - usually the reporting interval - to be more useful than measuring from boot time, particularly when there's a thread responding to user input (eg from the Zephyr shell, a thread started by other hardware input etc). Such a thread may consume a substantial amount of cpu time while it's executing, but a statistic measured since boot would only report it as using a small percentage.

For example, I had a put together a tool to measure network stack jitter, which I would configure and start from a shell command.  At the same time I wanted to gauge cpu usage of threads in the network stack. 
If I started the test after some time of the device being on, all threads would report <1% usage, when in reality they had used closer to 20% during the reporting intervals.
